title: Your Rights at a Traffic Stop
hook_angle: Max gets pulled over and starts explaining his whole life story before the officer even asks a question.
key_points: You must show license, registration, and proof of insurance when asked, but you can politely decline to answer questions beyond that.
You can ask 'Am I free to go?' and whether you're being detained, though whether police need a warrant to search your car varies by situation.
Staying calm and keeping your hands visible protects you more than arguing on the roadside, where you can't win the legal fight anyway.
sections: The difference between detention and arrest
Why you fight the ticket in court, not the street

title: Getting Your Security Deposit Back
hook_angle: Max assumes his landlord can keep the deposit for 'normal wear and tear' like faded paint, which is usually not allowed.
key_points: Landlords can deduct for actual damage beyond normal wear and tear, not for ordinary aging of the unit.
Most US states set a deadline (often 14 to 30 days, varies by state) for returning the deposit with an itemized list of deductions.
Documenting the unit with photos at move-in and move-out is your strongest evidence if there's a dispute.
sections: Damage vs. normal wear and tear

title: How Small Claims Court Actually Works
hook_angle: Max thinks he needs to hire an expensive lawyer to sue his contractor for $3,000, when small claims is built for exactly this.
key_points: Small claims court handles money disputes under a dollar limit that varies by state (often $2,500 to $25,000).
You usually don't need a lawyer, and in many states lawyers aren't even allowed to appear.
Winning a judgment and actually collecting the money are two different steps, and collection is often the harder one.

Dollar limits that vary by state

title: Gym and Subscription Contract Traps
hook_angle: Max signed up for a 'free trial' and got charged for a year because he missed the auto-renewal he never noticed.
key_points: Auto-renewal and negative-option billing laws require clear disclosure and easy cancellation in many US states.
Gym contracts often have cooling-off cancellation windows and must allow cancellation for relocation or disability in some states.
Disputing an unauthorized recurring charge with your card issuer is a real and powerful backup tool.

title: Product Warranties Explained
hook_angle: Max is told his broken blender isn't covered because he didn't mail in the warranty card, which usually isn't required.
key_points: Express warranties are promises the seller makes; implied warranties of merchantability come automatically unless clearly disclaimed.
A federal law (Magnuson-Moss) says a company generally can't void your warranty just because you used third-party parts.
'As is' sales can waive implied warranties in many states, so read the sticker before you buy.

title: At-Will Employment and Wrongful Termination
hook_angle: Max believes he can only be fired 'for a good reason,' but most US employment is at-will, meaning either side can end it almost anytime.
key_points: In almost every US state, employment is at-will, so you can be fired for any reason or no reason, as long as it isn't illegal.
Illegal reasons include firing based on race, sex, religion, age, disability, or in retaliation for protected activity.
A written contract, union agreement, or company policy can override the at-will default.
sections: The illegal reasons that create exceptions
Contracts and handbooks that change the rules
What counts as proof of wrongful termination

title: Miranda Rights Myths Debunked
hook_angle: Max thinks his case gets thrown out because the officer didn't read him his rights the second the cuffs went on.
key_points: Miranda warnings are only required before custodial interrogation, not at the moment of every arrest.
If police don't read them when required, the usual remedy is that your statements can be suppressed, not that the whole case vanishes.
You have to clearly invoke the right to silence or a lawyer; staying quiet alone may not be enough.

title: What 'Pressing Charges' Really Means
hook_angle: Max threatens to 'press charges' on his neighbor, not realizing that decision belongs to the prosecutor, not to him.
key_points: Victims report crimes, but the government (a prosecutor) decides whether to file criminal charges.
A victim often can't simply 'drop' charges once the state decides to pursue a case.
Criminal cases are brought by the state; if you want money, that's usually a separate civil lawsuit.

title: Reading Your Lease in Plain English
hook_angle: Max signs a lease without reading it and later learns he agreed to pay for all repairs and waive his right to sue.
key_points: Key clauses to find: rent and late fees, who handles repairs, entry notice, and early-termination penalties.
Some lease clauses are unenforceable even if you signed them, because state law overrides them.
Verbal promises from a landlord usually don't count unless they're written into the lease.

title: Tenant Rights and Eviction Basics
hook_angle: Max comes home to find the locks changed and his stuff on the curb, which is almost always illegal 'self-help' eviction.
key_points: Landlords must go through a court process to evict; changing locks or shutting off utilities to force you out is illegal in virtually every state.
You're generally entitled to written notice and a chance to respond before a judge can order you out.
Notice periods and allowable reasons for eviction vary by state and sometimes by city.
sections: The court hearing and your defenses
Notice periods that vary by state
How an eviction affects your record

title: Getting Out of a Car Dealership Contract
hook_angle: Max assumes a federal 'three-day cooling-off rule' lets him return the car he bought yesterday, which usually does not apply to cars.
key_points: There is generally no automatic right to cancel a car purchase; the common 'cooling-off' idea mostly applies to door-to-door sales, not dealerships.
The deal is usually final once you sign and drive off, unless financing falls through under a 'yo-yo' clause.
Your real leverage is fraud, misrepresentation, or an undisclosed defect, which varies by state.

title: Your Rights Against Debt Collectors (FDCPA)
hook_angle: Max is getting calls at 6 a.m. and at his job, and he doesn't realize a federal law puts strict limits on how collectors can act.
key_points: The federal FDCPA bars third-party debt collectors from harassment, threats, and calling at unreasonable hours.
You can demand a collector stop contacting you in writing, and you can request written verification of the debt.
Collectors can't lie, impersonate lawyers, or threaten arrest for an ordinary unpaid bill.
sections: Your right to a debt verification letter
Suing a collector that breaks the rules

title: Your Options After a Speeding Ticket
hook_angle: Max just pays every ticket immediately, not realizing that paying is an admission of guilt that adds points to his license.
key_points: Paying a ticket is usually pleading guilty, which can add points and raise your insurance.
Options often include contesting it, requesting traffic school, or negotiating a lesser charge, which varies by state.
A delay, missing officer, or faulty equipment can sometimes be grounds to beat the ticket.

title: NDAs Explained
hook_angle: Max panics that an NDA he signed means he can never speak about anything, when they only cover defined confidential information.
key_points: An NDA protects specific confidential information, not everything you know or experience.
NDAs generally can't be used to silence you about illegal conduct, and some states limit NDAs covering harassment.
Overly broad or indefinite NDAs can be unenforceable depending on state law.

title: Wills and Dying Without One (Intestacy)
hook_angle: Max assumes his unmarried partner will inherit everything, but without a will, state intestacy law decides, and partners often get nothing.
key_points: If you die without a will, state 'intestacy' law decides who inherits, usually spouse and blood relatives first.
Unmarried partners and friends typically receive nothing under intestacy, no matter your wishes.
A valid will lets you choose heirs and name a guardian for your kids; requirements for a valid will vary by state.
sections: Who gets left out without a will
Will formalities that vary by state
Beneficiary designations that override a will

title: Power of Attorney, Explained Simply
hook_angle: Max thinks signing a power of attorney means he's giving away control of his life forever, when it can be limited and revoked.
key_points: A power of attorney lets someone act on your behalf; it can be broad or limited to one task.
A 'durable' power of attorney keeps working if you become incapacitated, which is its main purpose.
You can usually revoke it anytime while you're competent, and it ends at your death.

title: Jury Duty: What You Need to Know
hook_angle: Max tries to ignore his jury summons, not realizing that skipping it can actually lead to fines or contempt.
key_points: Jury duty is a legal obligation, and ignoring a summons can result in penalties that vary by state.
Your employer generally can't fire you for serving, though pay-during-service rules vary by state.
You can request to be excused or postponed for genuine hardship, but you have to ask, not just skip.

title: Defamation vs. Free Speech
hook_angle: Max thinks any mean review of his business is 'defamation,' but opinions and true statements generally aren't.
key_points: Defamation requires a false statement of fact that harms reputation; pure opinion and true statements don't count.
Public figures must also prove 'actual malice,' a much higher bar than private individuals face.
The First Amendment limits the government, not private platforms, so a company removing your post isn't censorship in the legal sense.
sections: What the First Amendment does and doesn't cover

title: Copyright and Fair Use Basics
hook_angle: Max thinks adding 'no copyright intended' to his video magically makes using someone's song legal.
key_points: Copyright protects original creative work automatically; disclaimers like 'no copyright intended' have no legal effect.
Fair use is a flexible four-factor defense, not a fixed rule like 'under 30 seconds is fine.'
Giving credit is polite but does not by itself make unlicensed use legal.

title: Stand Your Ground vs. Duty to Retreat
hook_angle: Max assumes self-defense works the same everywhere, but whether you must retreat before using force varies a lot by state.
key_points: Self-defense generally requires a reasonable, proportional response to an imminent threat.
Some states impose a 'duty to retreat' if you can safely do so, while 'stand your ground' states do not; this varies by state.
The 'castle doctrine' commonly gives extra protection when defending your own home.

title: Prenups: Myths and Reality
hook_angle: Max thinks asking for a prenup means he's planning the divorce, when it's really just deciding the rules in advance.
key_points: A prenup sets out how assets and debts are handled if a marriage ends, mostly for property, not daily life.
Prenups generally can't predetermine child custody or child support, which courts decide based on the child's best interest.
Full financial disclosure and independent review help a prenup hold up; enforceability rules vary by state.

title: Child Custody Basics
hook_angle: Max assumes mothers automatically get custody, but courts decide based on the child's best interest, not the parent's gender.
key_points: Courts decide custody using the 'best interests of the child' standard, not an automatic preference for either parent.
Legal custody (decision-making) and physical custody (where the child lives) are separate and can be split.
Custody orders can be modified when circumstances change; specific factors and rules vary by state.
sections: Modifying an order later (varies by state)

title: Your Overtime Pay Rights
hook_angle: Max is told he's 'salaried' so he gets no overtime, but a title alone doesn't decide whether you're exempt.
key_points: Under federal law, non-exempt employees generally earn 1.5x pay for hours over 40 in a week.
Being paid a salary or called a 'manager' doesn't automatically make you exempt; your actual duties and pay level matter.
Some states have stricter rules, like daily overtime, so protections can be greater than federal (varies by state).

title: What Your HOA Can and Can't Do
hook_angle: Max thinks his HOA can do absolutely anything, including take his house over an unpaid $200 fine overnight.
key_points: HOAs get their power from the recorded covenants (CC&Rs) you agreed to when buying, not unlimited authority.
HOAs can fine and place liens, and in some states even foreclose, but usually only through a defined legal process.
Members typically have rights to notice, to inspect records, and to challenge rules; specifics vary by state.

title: Renter's Insurance: Do You Need It?
hook_angle: Max assumes his landlord's insurance covers his stolen laptop, but that policy only protects the building, not his stuff.
key_points: A landlord's insurance covers the building, not a tenant's personal belongings.
Renter's insurance typically covers your belongings, liability if someone is hurt, and living costs if the unit becomes unlivable.
Some landlords can require renter's insurance in the lease, which is generally allowed.

title: Expungement: Clearing Your Record
hook_angle: Max believes a dismissed charge automatically disappears, but records often stick around until you actively clear them.
key_points: Expungement or sealing can remove or hide certain records, but it usually doesn't happen automatically; you must petition.
Which offenses qualify, and the waiting period, varies a lot by state.
Even after expungement, some agencies (like certain licensing bodies) may still see the record.

title: Statute of Limitations, Explained
hook_angle: Max waits five years to sue over a car crash, then learns he missed the deadline and lost his case automatically.
key_points: A statute of limitations is a deadline to file a lawsuit or bring charges; miss it and you usually lose the right.
Time limits differ by type of claim and by state, so there's no single universal number.
The clock can sometimes pause ('toll'), for example when the harmed person is a minor.

title: DUI Stop Basics
hook_angle: Max thinks refusing a breathalyzer has no downside, but 'implied consent' laws mean refusal can trigger an automatic license suspension.
key_points: Under 'implied consent' laws in every state, refusing a chemical test after a lawful DUI arrest can suspend your license.
Field sobriety tests (walking a line) are often voluntary, unlike the post-arrest chemical test; rules vary by state.
You generally have the right to remain silent and to request a lawyer.

title: Airline Passenger Rights
hook_angle: Max gets bumped from an overbooked flight and assumes he's just out of luck, when he may be owed compensation.
key_points: If you're involuntarily bumped from an oversold flight, US rules may entitle you to cash compensation, not just a voucher.
For cancellations, you're generally entitled to a refund if you choose not to fly, even on nonrefundable tickets.
Tarmac delay rules limit how long airlines can keep you waiting on the plane.

title: The Warranty of Habitability
hook_angle: Max thinks he has no choice but to live with no heat in winter because 'the lease didn't promise heat.'
key_points: In most US states, landlords must keep rentals livable, with basics like heat, water, and working plumbing, even if the lease is silent.
You generally must notify the landlord and give a reasonable chance to fix the problem first.
Remedies like repair-and-deduct or rent withholding exist but have strict rules that vary by state.

title: Noncompete Agreements
hook_angle: Max is afraid he can never work in his field again because of a noncompete, but many are limited or even unenforceable.
key_points: Noncompetes restrict where you can work after leaving a job, but courts often won't enforce overly broad ones.
Some states ban or heavily limit noncompetes, especially for lower-wage workers, so enforceability varies by state.
Even where allowed, a noncompete usually must be reasonable in time, geography, and scope.
sections: States that ban or limit them (varies by state)
What happens if you breach one

title: Filing a Police Report
hook_angle: Max thinks filing a police report automatically means someone gets arrested and charged, which isn't how it works.
key_points: A police report documents an incident; it doesn't by itself guarantee an arrest or charges.
Reports can be important for insurance claims, protective orders, and creating a record.
Knowingly filing a false report is itself a crime, so stick to the facts.

title: Suing Someone: The Real Process
hook_angle: Max expects a dramatic trial next week, not realizing most lawsuits drag on for months and usually settle before trial.
key_points: A lawsuit starts with filing a complaint and formally serving the other side, not with a courtroom showdown.
Discovery (exchanging evidence) is the long, expensive middle stage, and most cases settle before trial.
Winning doesn't guarantee payment; collecting on a judgment is a separate challenge.

title: Landmark Cases Told Simply
hook_angle: Max can quote 'you have the right to remain silent' from TV but has no idea it comes from a real Supreme Court case.
key_points: Miranda v. Arizona created the warning police must give before custodial questioning.
Gideon v. Wainwright guaranteed a free lawyer for defendants who can't afford one in serious criminal cases.
Tinker v. Des Moines held that students don't shed their free-speech rights at the schoolhouse gate.

title: Identity Theft: What to Do First
hook_angle: Max sees a strange credit card account in his name and freezes, not knowing the concrete steps that actually stop the bleeding.
key_points: Act fast: place a fraud alert or credit freeze, and report to the FTC at IdentityTheft.gov for a recovery plan.
You're generally not liable for most fraudulent charges if you report them promptly.
File a police report and dispute fraudulent accounts in writing to create a paper trail.

title: Workplace Harassment: Know the Line
hook_angle: Max assumes a rude boss is automatically illegal harassment, but the law targets harassment based on protected traits, not general jerks.
key_points: Illegal harassment is unwelcome conduct based on a protected trait (like sex, race, or religion) that's severe or pervasive.
A single rude boss or general unfairness usually isn't illegal unless it's tied to a protected characteristic.
Reporting through your employer's process and keeping records matters, and retaliation for complaining is separately illegal.
sections: Quid pro quo vs. hostile environment

title: Consumer Lemon Laws
hook_angle: Max assumes any used car that breaks down qualifies as a 'lemon,' but lemon laws are narrower than people think.
key_points: Lemon laws generally cover new vehicles with a substantial defect the dealer can't fix after a reasonable number of tries.
What qualifies, and whether used cars are covered, varies by state.
You usually must give the manufacturer a fair chance to repair before you have a claim.

title: What Being a Cosigner Really Means
hook_angle: Max cosigns his nephew's car loan thinking he's just 'vouching,' not realizing he's fully on the hook if the nephew stops paying.
key_points: A cosigner is equally responsible for the full debt, not just a backup reference.
If the main borrower misses payments, it hits your credit and the lender can come after you.
Getting released from a cosigned loan is hard and usually requires the lender's agreement.

title: Restraining Orders, Explained
hook_angle: Max thinks a restraining order is instant and permanent, but it usually starts temporary and needs a court hearing to continue.
key_points: A protective order often starts as a temporary emergency order, then a hearing decides whether it becomes longer-term.
The process, available types, and duration vary by state.
Violating a restraining order is a crime, even if the protected person invites contact.

title: Your Rights to Medical Records and Consent
hook_angle: Max assumes the hospital owns his records and can refuse to share them, but federal law gives him a right to his own records.
key_points: Under federal law (HIPAA), you generally have the right to access and get copies of your own medical records.
Informed consent means a provider must explain risks and alternatives before most treatments.
You can usually refuse treatment as a competent adult, with narrow exceptions.
